tagline: A Fortress for the Family Photos
dek: Online backup for home computers and small businesses, sold for a flat yearly fee and pitched hard on talk radio.
lede: Carbonite sold peace of mind. For a flat yearly price, its software quietly copied everything on a home computer to servers in a data center, so a dead hard drive or a stolen laptop no longer meant lost photos and tax returns. By the summer of 2011 broadband was everywhere, the cloud was a household word, and Carbonite had become one of the most familiar voices on American talk radio, selling backup to people who had never thought about it.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: David Friend and Jeff Flowers, serial founders from the Boston tech scene, bet that ordinary people would pay a small subscription to never think about backup again. Most consumers had no backup at all. Carbonite made it automatic and unlimited, and spent heavily on radio and podcast ads to reach people who would never read a tech review. Later it added plans for small businesses, which proved to be the steadier customers.

sections.heading: Into the Vault
sections.body: Carbonite priced its IPO at $10 a share in August 2011, in a jittery market, and traded unevenly for years as consumer growth slowed. The company shifted toward business customers and bought several rivals, including Webroot in 2019. Later that year OpenText agreed to acquire Carbonite for about $1.42 billion, folding the backup pioneer into a large enterprise software group.

dek: A real estate website that put an estimated value on nearly every home in America and made house hunting a hobby.
lede: Zillow opened the front door of the American housing market. Its site showed listings, sales histories and a computed value, the Zestimate, for tens of millions of homes, including ones not for sale. When it filed to go public in 2011, housing was still deep in the wreckage of the financial crisis. Yet people kept looking, often at their own homes and their neighbors', and Zillow had become one of the most visited real estate sites in the country.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Rich Barton had already turned travel booking into a consumer product at Expedia. With Lloyd Frink he bet that real estate data, long held close by agents and listing services, could be opened up to everyone. The Zestimate, launched in 2006, was the hook: a free, instant and sometimes argued-over number for any address. Zillow made its money from agents and advertisers who wanted to reach all those curious browsers.

sections.heading: The Road to the Bell
sections.body: Zillow priced its IPO at $20 a share in July 2011 and traded well above that on its first day. It bought rival Trulia in 2015 and became the dominant home search site in the United States. A move into buying and flipping homes directly, Zillow Offers, ended in 2021 with large losses. The company returned to its roots as a marketplace and remains publicly traded.

dek: An online marketplace for vacation rentals, connecting travelers with owners of beach houses, cabins and condos.
lede: HomeAway gathered the scattered world of vacation rentals into one place. Before it, renting a beach house meant classified ads, phone calls and word of mouth. HomeAway bought up listing sites such as VRBO and charged owners to advertise their homes to travelers. When it filed in 2011, Airbnb was still a young startup, and HomeAway was the largest vacation rental marketplace in the world.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Brian Sharples and Carl Shepherd started in Austin in 2005 with a roll-up plan. They raised a large amount of venture money early and used it to buy established rental sites in the United States and Europe, including VRBO. The business model was simple: owners paid a yearly subscription to list their properties, and travelers browsed for free. The scale of its listings drew travelers, and travelers drew more owners.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: HomeAway priced its IPO at $27 a share in June 2011 and closed its first day well above that. Over the next few years it began to charge travelers a booking fee as Airbnb grew into a serious rival. In 2015 Expedia bought HomeAway for about $3.9 billion. The business later took the name of one of its oldest pieces, Vrbo.

cover.theme: a fisherman's cottage by the water (a vacation home)

dek: The professional social network, where people kept an online résumé and recruiters came looking for them.
lede: LinkedIn turned the business card and the résumé into a living network. Members kept an online profile of their career and connected with colleagues, and recruiters paid to search that map of the working world. By 2011 it had more than 100 million members. It was the first major American social network to go public, a year ahead of Facebook, and the market treated its listing as a test of the whole social media wave.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Reid Hoffman, an early PayPal executive, started LinkedIn with a small group of friends from SocialNet and PayPal, and launched it in 2003. The bet was that professionals would put their real identities and work histories online if the network helped them get jobs and deals. LinkedIn made money three ways: recruiting tools, advertising and premium subscriptions. The recruiting business became the engine.

sections.heading: The Road to the Bell
sections.body: LinkedIn priced its shares at $45 in May 2011 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. The stock more than doubled on its first day of trading. The company grew steadily as a public company and bought Lynda.com in 2015. In 2016 Microsoft acquired LinkedIn for $26.2 billion, its largest purchase at the time, and kept it running as an independent brand.

dek: Wi-Fi in airports, then wireless networks for stadiums, military bases and buildings.
lede: Boingo was the name on the screen when a traveler opened a laptop at the gate. The company ran paid Wi-Fi in many of the busiest airports in the United States and resold access to hotspots around the world. By 2011, smartphones were changing the business. Boingo was also building cellular antenna systems inside airports and stadiums, so that phone carriers could serve the crowds there.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Sky Dayton, who had founded the internet provider EarthLink, started Boingo in 2001, when public Wi-Fi was new and scattered. His bet was that one account could work across thousands of hotspots, the way a phone worked across cell towers. Boingo won long contracts to run the networks in major airports, which gave it steady and defensible positions. Roaming deals with other hotspot operators let Boingo customers log in far beyond its own locations.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Boingo priced its IPO at $13.50 a share in May 2011. Free Wi-Fi spread through airports and coffee shops, so the company leaned into building wireless infrastructure for venues, carriers and military bases. In 2021 it was acquired by an investment group led by Digital Colony and taken private. Its long airport contracts and military base networks gave it steady revenue, even as consumer Wi-Fi fees faded.

cover.theme: kites in the sky (signals in the air)
cover.artwork: Kites of Fukuroi and Distant View of Akiba in Totomi Province (Enshu Akiba enkei Fukuroi tako), from the series "One Hundred Famous Views in the Various Provinces (Shokoku meisho hyakkei)"

dek: Software that mortgage lenders used to take a home loan from application to closing.
lede: Ellie Mae built the software behind the American mortgage. Its Encompass system let lenders and brokers take in an application, check it, price it and close it, while its network connected them to the appraisers, credit bureaus and investors involved in every loan. It filed to go public in 2011, while the housing market was still recovering, and few investors wanted anything to do with mortgages.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Sig Anderman and Limin Hu started the company in 1997, when a mortgage still traveled by fax and courier. They bet that loan origination could move onto a single shared platform, and that lenders would pay per loan for it. Ellie Mae grew by selling Encompass to small and midsize lenders, then to larger ones as regulation made careful records essential.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Ellie Mae priced its IPO at $6 a share in April 2011, below its planned range, and listed on the NYSE Amex exchange. As refinancing and new rules drove lenders to its software, the stock rose many times over. Thoma Bravo took the company private in 2019 for about $3.7 billion. In 2020 Intercontinental Exchange bought it for about $11 billion.

cover.theme: a doorway (the way into a home)

dek: An online broker for retail foreign exchange trading, best known for its FOREX.com platform.
lede: GAIN Capital opened the currency market to individual traders. Through FOREX.com and other platforms, customers could trade dollars, euros and yen from home, with leverage, around the clock. By late 2010 retail forex was a fast-growing and lightly understood corner of finance. New American rules were just beginning to cap leverage and tighten oversight. Most of its customers were individuals trading from home, drawn by low minimums and round-the-clock markets.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Mark Galant founded GAIN in 1999 with a simple idea: the professional foreign exchange market could be packaged for individuals online. The company acted as the counterparty to many customer trades and earned money from spreads. It grew in the United States, then expanded into the United Kingdom, Japan and other markets. Retail forex was young and loosely regulated when GAIN started, and the company grew into one of the largest brokers in the field.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: GAIN priced its IPO at $9 a share in December 2010 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. It bought rivals including GFT and City Index, but tighter regulation and low currency volatility weighed on the business. In 2020 it was acquired by INTL FCStone, which renamed itself StoneX. Its share price spent most of the decade below the offering price, and the sale to StoneX ended its run as a public company.

dek: A software and investment platform that independent financial advisers used to manage their clients' money.
lede: Envestnet worked behind the financial adviser's desk. Its platform let advisers open accounts, build portfolios from many managers, rebalance them and report to clients, all in one place. As more advisers left big brokerages to go independent, they needed the tools those firms had provided. Envestnet filed to go public in the summer of 2010, as markets were recovering from the crisis.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Judson Bergman started Envestnet in 1999 with a bet on the independent adviser. He saw that wealth management was moving toward fee-based accounts and away from commissions, and that advisers would pay for technology that made it run. Envestnet charged a small fee on the assets on its platform, so it grew as markets and its adviser base grew. Its open architecture let advisers choose from many outside money managers, which set it apart from captive brokerage platforms.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Envestnet priced its IPO at $9 a share in July 2010 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. It grew through acquisitions, including the data business Yodlee in 2015, and assets on its platform rose into the trillions of dollars. In 2024 Bain Capital took the company private in a deal valued at about $4.5 billion. The Yodlee deal gave Envestnet a large store of financial account data, which it sold to banks and fintech companies.

cover.theme: a harvest field (wealth grown over time)

dek: Online marketing for small local businesses, sold door to door by a large field sales force.
lede: ReachLocal sold the internet to Main Street. Plumbers, dentists and restaurants knew they needed customers to find them on Google, but few knew how to buy search ads. ReachLocal's salespeople signed them up, then its software spread their budgets across search engines and tracked the calls that came back. In 2010 the company was growing fast across the United States and abroad.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Zorik Gordon and Michael Kline founded ReachLocal in 2004. They bet that small businesses would pay a premium to have someone else handle online advertising for them. The company built a large sales force and its own technology for managing campaigns. It earned its margin on the difference between what clients paid and the cost of the media it bought. Its pitch was simple: a business owner paid one monthly budget, and ReachLocal handled the rest.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: ReachLocal priced its IPO at $13 a share in May 2010. Over time, small businesses found cheaper ways to advertise, and the costly sales model became a burden. Revenue fell and the stock sank far below its offering price. In 2016 Gannett, the newspaper publisher, bought ReachLocal for about $156 million. Its decline mirrored a broader shift, as Google and Facebook made self-serve advertising easy for even the smallest shops.

cover.theme: a busy street of shops (local business)

dek: Online fundraising, email and donor management software for nonprofit organizations.
lede: Convio helped charities raise money on the internet. Its hosted software ran donation pages, email campaigns, event registrations and donor databases for nonprofits of every size, from local food banks to national health charities. By 2010 online giving was growing every year, and charities were learning to treat their websites as a front door for supporters. Its customers ranged from small community groups to some of the largest charities in the country.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Convio started in Austin in 1999 with a bet that nonprofits would need the same online tools that retailers were adopting, but could not build them alone. It sold its software as a subscription service, years before that model was common. Charity walks and runs, where participants raise money from friends online, became one of its signature products. Its tools also helped charities keep in touch with donors between campaigns, through email newsletters and online advocacy.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Convio priced its IPO at $9 a share in April 2010. It grew modestly as a public company in a market led by Blackbaud, the larger nonprofit software maker. In 2012 Blackbaud agreed to buy Convio for about $275 million and combined the two product lines. Blackbaud kept parts of the Convio platform, which became the basis of its Luminate products for large nonprofits. The deal joined the two best-known names in nonprofit software.

cover.artwork: New York Charities—St Barnabas House, 304 Mulberry Street

dek: Online investment advice and managed accounts for workers saving in 401(k) plans.
lede: Financial Engines brought Nobel-prize finance to the office 401(k). It offered workers advice on how to invest their retirement savings and, for a fee, would manage those accounts for them. It sold through employers and plan providers rather than directly to the public. When it filed in early 2010, the crisis had just wiped out much of many workers' savings, and the case for professional help felt urgent.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: William Sharpe, who won the Nobel Prize in economics in 1990, co-founded the company in 1996 with securities law professor Joseph Grundfest and venture capitalist Craig Johnson. Their bet was that rigorous portfolio models could be delivered cheaply over the internet to millions of ordinary savers. The Pension Protection Act of 2006, which encouraged automatic advice in retirement plans, opened the door wider.

sections.heading: The Road to the Bell
sections.body: Financial Engines priced its IPO at $12 a share in March 2010, one of the first technology offerings after the crisis, and rose sharply on its first day. Assets under its management grew for years. In 2018 Hellman & Friedman bought the company for about $3 billion and merged it with Edelman Financial. The combined firm brought together online advice for workplace savers and in-person planning for wealthier clients.

cover.theme: a model steam engine (a steady engine)

tagline: Where the Customer Meets the Road
dek: Performance marketing that found customers for colleges, insurers and lenders and was paid by the lead.
lede: QuinStreet sold customers, not ad space. It ran websites and campaigns that drew in people shopping for a degree, an insurance policy or a loan, then passed their interest to schools and companies that paid per qualified lead or click. In early 2010 its biggest market was for-profit education, which was booming as unemployed adults went back to school. Few consumers knew its name, though many had filled out one of its forms.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Doug Valenti and Bronwyn Syiek founded QuinStreet in 1999. Their bet was that advertisers would rather pay for results than for impressions, and that a company could earn a margin by matching high-intent shoppers to buyers. QuinStreet built and bought content sites in its chosen fields and invested in the data needed to price each lead. Advertisers liked that they paid only for results, and QuinStreet carried the risk of turning ad spending into qualified leads.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: QuinStreet priced its IPO at $15 a share in February 2010. New federal rules on for-profit colleges soon cut into its largest business, and the stock fell. The company shifted toward insurance and financial services, where demand grew. It remains publicly traded on the Nasdaq. Its model, paid for results rather than for attention, stayed much the same through the changes in its markets.

cover.artwork: Morning, Crossroads of the Forts de Marlotte

dek: A subscription website of digitized historical records where families traced their genealogy online.
lede: Ancestry.com put the archive in the living room. It digitized billions of records, such as census rolls, ship manifests and military files, and sold subscriptions to people building their family trees. It filed to go public in late 2009, during a deep recession, with steadily rising subscribers and a popular television tie-in, Who Do You Think You Are? Many subscribers stayed for years, adding branches as new records came online.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The company's roots go back to a genealogy publisher in Utah, a state with a deep tradition of family history research. Its bet was that the hobby of genealogy could become a mass market if the records were searchable from home. Ancestry spent years and large sums scanning and indexing records, which gave it a collection rivals could not easily copy.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Ancestry priced its IPO at $13.50 a share in November 2009. Subscribers kept growing, and the company began selling DNA tests that would later become a major business. In 2012 a group led by Permira took Ancestry private for about $1.6 billion. Blackstone bought the company in 2020. AncestryDNA, launched in 2012, sold millions of saliva kits and linked customers to relatives they had never met.

dek: An online store for vitamins, supplements and natural products, many sold under its own brands.
lede: Vitacost sold vitamins and health products online at low prices. Alongside national brands, it made and sold its own lines of supplements, which gave it better margins. It shipped from its own warehouses to customers across the country. It went public in September 2009, a time when few retailers were growing and online shopping kept gaining ground. Customers liked its deep discounts and wide range of brands that local stores did not carry.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Wayne Gorsek founded the business in 1994 as a catalog company. He bet that customers who bought supplements regularly would shop by price and convenience, and that a direct seller could beat the markup of health food stores. Vitacost moved online early and invested in its own manufacturing. Free shipping thresholds and frequent coupons kept customers reordering every few months.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Vitacost priced its IPO at $12 a share in September 2009. Its years as a public company were difficult, with management turnover, accounting questions and losses. In 2014 the grocery chain Kroger bought Vitacost for about $280 million to strengthen its online health business. Kroger kept Vitacost running as an online store and used its warehouses and know-how to ship health products to its own shoppers.

dek: Online restaurant reservations for diners and table management software for restaurants.
lede: OpenTable let diners book a restaurant table online in seconds. Behind that simple service was a computer system that sat at the host stand of thousands of restaurants, managing seating and reservations. Restaurants paid a monthly fee for the system and a small charge for each diner the website sent. It went public in May 2009, in the depths of the recession, when restaurants were hurting and few tech companies dared to list.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Chuck Templeton founded the company in 1998 after struggling to book a dinner reservation by phone. The bet was that both sides needed help: diners wanted to book at any hour, and restaurants wanted to fill seats and know their guests. OpenTable spent years installing its system restaurant by restaurant, city by city, before the network effects took hold. Its early markets were San Francisco and a handful of other big cities.

sections.heading: The Road to the Bell
sections.body: OpenTable priced its IPO at $20 a share in May 2009 and rose sharply on its first day, a bright spot in a grim market. The company expanded to more cities and to mobile booking. In 2014 Priceline, now Booking Holdings, bought OpenTable for about $2.6 billion. The deal gave Priceline a foothold in dining, and OpenTable kept growing in cities around the world.

cover.artwork: Lunch at the Restaurant Fournaise (The Rowers' Lunch)

tagline: Watching Which Way the Wind Blows
dek: Network and systems monitoring software sold online to IT administrators at low prices.
lede: SolarWinds made tools for the people who keep networks running. Its software watched routers, servers and applications and warned administrators when something went wrong. It sold differently from most enterprise software: no large sales force, just downloadable trials, low prices and a strong online community. It filed to go public in 2009, one of the few tech listings of that bleak year.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Donald Yonce and his son David started the company in Tulsa, Oklahoma, in 1999. Their bet was that IT staff would buy practical, affordable tools themselves, without long sales cycles. They built a loyal following through free tools and online forums, and the company later moved its headquarters to Austin. Its prices were low enough that an administrator could often buy without asking a committee.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: SolarWinds priced its IPO at $12.50 a share in May 2009. Silver Lake and Thoma Bravo took it private in 2016 and listed it again in 2018. In 2020 hackers compromised its Orion software in one of the most serious cyberattacks in American history. In 2025 Turn/River Capital took the company private for about $4.4 billion. Through all of it, its products stayed a fixture in IT departments.

fate: Taken private by Apollo, 2016 ($4.3B); relisted 2020 (NASDAQ: RXT)
dek: Managed web hosting and, later, cloud computing, sold on the promise of 'Fanatical Support.'
lede: Rackspace ran other companies' servers and answered the phone when they broke. Customers rented dedicated machines in Rackspace data centers and paid extra for a team that managed them day and night. The company called this 'Fanatical Support' and built its culture around it. When it went public in August 2008, the financial system was weeks from collapse, and Amazon's new cloud was beginning to change what hosting meant.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Three Trinity University students, Richard Yoo, Dirk Elmendorf and Pat Condon, started the company in San Antonio in 1998, and investor Graham Weston soon joined to lead it. The bet was that most businesses did not want to run their own servers, and that service, not hardware, would set a hosting company apart. Rackspace grew quickly by serving small and midsize businesses that had no IT staff.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Rackspace priced its IPO at $12.50 a share in August 2008 on the New York Stock Exchange. It launched a cloud business and co-founded the OpenStack project with NASA in 2010. Competition from Amazon, Microsoft and Google squeezed it, and Apollo took it private in 2016 for about $4.3 billion. It returned to the public market in 2020. Today it mostly helps customers run workloads on the big public clouds.

tagline: Running the Business in the Clouds
dek: Accounting and business management software delivered over the internet to growing companies.
lede: NetSuite put a company's books in the browser. Its software handled accounting, orders, inventory and customer records in a single system, hosted on its own servers and sold by subscription. In 2007, enterprise software still mostly meant installing large packages on company computers. NetSuite was one of the first to show that the core financial system of a business could live in the cloud.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Evan Goldberg, a former Oracle executive, founded the company in 1998 with backing from Larry Ellison. The bet was that small and midsize businesses would trade the cost and hassle of installed software for one integrated online service. NetSuite spent years building out its product while the market for cloud software slowly matured. Ellison's backing gave the young company money and credibility while it waited for the market.

sections.heading: The Road to the Bell
sections.body: NetSuite priced its IPO at $26 a share in December 2007 on the New York Stock Exchange, under the ticker N. The stock fell hard in the 2008 crash. Growth returned as cloud software won acceptance. In 2016 Oracle bought NetSuite for about $9.3 billion. By then NetSuite served thousands of midsize businesses, and the deal made Oracle a major player in cloud business software.

tagline: The Schoolroom at the Kitchen Table
dek: Online curriculum and full-time virtual public schools for kindergarten through high school students.
lede: K12 brought public school into the home. It created an online curriculum and ran virtual charter schools for states and districts, so students could take a full course load from a computer at home with certified teachers on the other end. When it went public in December 2007, online learning was still unfamiliar to most parents, and the idea of a public company running schools drew sharp debate.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Ron Packard, a former banker and McKinsey consultant, founded K12 in 2000 with backing from Knowledge Universe, and former Education Secretary William Bennett was its first chairman. The bet was that families wanted more choice in schooling, and that a strong online curriculum could serve students anywhere. K12 earned most of its revenue from public funds that followed students to its schools.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: K12 priced its IPO at $18 a share in December 2007 on the New York Stock Exchange. Enrollment grew for years, along with criticism of student results at some of its schools. In 2020 the company renamed itself Stride, and the pandemic sent enrollment sharply higher. It remains publicly traded under its original ticker. Its business now spans online public schools, private online schools and career training programs.

dek: A collection of niche websites and online communities, from car buying to travel forums to legal directories.
lede: Internet Brands was a company of many websites. It began as CarsDirect, a site for buying a car online, then bought and built hundreds of focused sites and communities on cars, home improvement, travel, health and law. Each was small, but together they drew a large audience and steady advertising. It went public in November 2007, just before the financial crisis.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: CarsDirect was started at Bill Gross's Idealab in 1998, with Scott Painter, as one of the early bets that people would buy big-ticket items online. When that market proved hard, the company changed course. It began buying established enthusiast sites and forums cheaply, then ran them on shared technology and sold advertising across the network. The model worked because each site already had a loyal, specific audience.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Internet Brands priced its IPO at $8 a share in November 2007 on the Nasdaq. In 2010 Hellman & Friedman bought the company for about $640 million. KKR later acquired it, and in 2017 Internet Brands bought WebMD, another company in this directory. The company kept growing by buying communities and specialist sites, and the WebMD deal made it a major force in online health.

cover.theme: a shop front (a network of niche sites)

dek: An online university system that began by teaching active-duty military personnel.
lede: American Public Education ran an online university built for people in uniform. Its American Military University and American Public University offered degrees that soldiers, sailors and veterans could complete from anywhere, often paid for by military tuition assistance. When it filed in 2007, for-profit online colleges were growing fast, and APEI stood out for its low tuition and its military focus.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: James Etter, a retired Marine officer, founded American Military University in 1991. The bet was that service members, who move often and deploy far from campus, needed a university that went with them. The school kept its prices close to the military's tuition assistance cap, which made it an easy choice for many students. Its admissions were open and courses started every month, which suited students on shifting military schedules.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: APEI priced its IPO at $20 a share in November 2007 on the Nasdaq, and the stock rose strongly in its early years. Enrollment later slowed as for-profit education faced tighter federal rules. The company expanded into nursing education through acquisitions and remains publicly traded. The American Public University System remains its core, and it serves many civilian students alongside service members.

tagline: The Bell That Calls You Back
dek: Hosted software for automated outbound calls, texts and emails, used for collections and customer reminders.
lede: SoundBite ran the automated messages companies send to their customers. Banks, utilities, retailers and collection agencies used its hosted system to place reminder calls, payment notices and alerts by voice, text and email. It sold the service over the internet, so clients needed no equipment of their own. It filed to go public in 2007, when hosted software was still a new way to sell.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: SoundBite started in 2000 with a bet that outbound customer contact could move from call center hardware to a hosted service. Its first big market was collections, where reaching more people at the right time had a direct value. It later added more channels and pitched its service for friendlier messages, such as appointment reminders and fraud alerts. Clients paid by usage, so revenue rose with each campaign they ran.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: SoundBite priced its IPO at $8 a share in November 2007, weeks before the financial crisis began to bite. Its stock stayed low for most of its time as a public company. In 2013 Genesys, the contact center software maker, bought SoundBite for about $100 million. Genesys folded SoundBite's outbound tools into its larger contact center platform, giving clients one place to handle calls in both directions.

cover.theme: a bell being rung (a call to customers)

dek: A Mexican telephone, internet and cable company that competed with Telmex in local service.
lede: Maxcom was a challenger in Mexican telecom. It offered local phone, internet and later pay television to homes and small businesses in Mexico City, Puebla and other cities, in a market long dominated by Telmex. It listed its shares on the New York Stock Exchange in 2007, when emerging markets were in favor and investors were looking for growth in Latin America.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Maxcom was founded in 1996, after Mexico opened local telephone service to competition. The bet was that a nimble new carrier could win customers from a slow incumbent by building modern networks in selected cities and bundling services. It invested heavily in its own lines and fiber. Like many challengers, it faced the hard economics of building physical networks street by street.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Maxcom priced its New York listing at $17.50 per American depositary share in October 2007. The financial crisis and fierce competition hurt the business, and the company went through debt troubles and restructuring. It delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2014. Its shares continued to trade in Mexico and over the counter in the United States after that. The company never matched the growth its 2007 investors had hoped for.

dek: Email marketing software for small businesses and nonprofits, with templates, mailing lists and coaching.
lede: Constant Contact taught small businesses to send email newsletters. Its online service gave a florist, a dentist or a church easy templates, a place to keep a mailing list and reports on who opened each message. The company backed this with seminars and phone coaching across the country. By 2007 it had tens of thousands of customers paying monthly. Its customers were mostly very small organizations.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Randy Parker founded the company in 1995 as Roving Software. The bet was that small organizations wanted to keep in touch with their customers but lacked the skills of big marketers. Gail Goodman, who became chief executive in 1999, focused the company on email marketing and built its sales engine around free trials and radio ads. Customer service and education became central to how it sold.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Constant Contact priced its IPO at $16 a share in October 2007 on the Nasdaq. It added social media and event tools and kept growing through the downturn. In 2016 Endurance International Group bought the company for about $1.1 billion. Endurance kept Constant Contact as a separate brand, and it later became a separate company again under private equity ownership.

cover.artwork: Messenger with a Letter, from the series "Elegant Five-needled Pine (Furyu goyo no matsu)"

tagline: The Road to the Great Market
dek: Latin America's largest online marketplace, later its largest e-commerce and payments company.
lede: MercadoLibre built the marketplace of Latin America. Its site let people in Argentina, Brazil, Mexico and other countries buy and sell new and used goods online, and its payment service, MercadoPago, helped them trust strangers with their money. When it went public in August 2007, it was one of very few Latin American internet companies to list in New York.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Marcos Galperin started MercadoLibre in 1999 while studying at Stanford Business School, and launched it in Buenos Aires with Hernán Kazah. The bet was that e-commerce in Latin America needed a local champion that understood its markets, currencies and logistics. In 2001 eBay bought a stake in the company and agreed to stay out of the region. The company later moved its base to Montevideo, Uruguay.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: MercadoLibre priced its IPO at $18 a share in August 2007 on the Nasdaq. It built its own shipping network and turned MercadoPago into a major fintech business. It became one of the most valuable companies in Latin America and remains publicly traded. Its fintech arm now offers digital wallets, loans and payments across the region, far beyond its marketplace.

cover.theme: the road to market (a great marketplace)

tagline: The Watchful Eye at the Door
dek: Online background checks and employment screening for large employers.
lede: HireRight checked people's pasts before they started a new job. Employers ordered criminal, education, employment and drug screens through its website, and HireRight gathered the results from courts and records across the country and abroad. It worked mostly for large companies that hired in volume. When it filed in 2007, background screening had become standard practice in American hiring. Its customers included many Fortune 500 companies.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: HireRight was founded in 1995 with a bet that the slow, paper-based business of employment screening could move onto the internet. It built software that plugged into employers' hiring systems, so a check could start with a click and the results could flow straight back. That integration helped it win large corporate accounts. International checks became a strength as global companies screened candidates in many countries.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: HireRight priced its IPO at $15 a share in August 2007 on the Nasdaq. Its time as a public company was short. In 2008 US Investigations Services, a large provider of government background checks, bought HireRight for $19.75 a share in cash. The HireRight name lived on. It later returned to the public market as a separate company and was taken private again.

cover.artwork: Ornament with Owl Mocked by Day Birds

dek: A type foundry and font licensing business whose typefaces ran inside printers, phones and software.
lede: Monotype owned many of the letters the world reads. Its library included famous typefaces such as Helvetica and Times New Roman, and it licensed fonts and font technology to the makers of printers, phones, cars and software. In 2007 most people never saw its name, but its type appeared on billions of screens and pages. Its fonts were built into many of the laser printers in offices around the world.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Monotype traces its roots to the 1880s, when Tolbert Lanston invented a machine that cast metal type one letter at a time. The company survived the move from hot metal to photo type to digital fonts by holding on to its library and its craft. Its modern bet was that fonts were intellectual property that device makers would license, one unit at a time.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Monotype Imaging priced its IPO at $12 a share in July 2007 on the Nasdaq. It bought Linotype, Fonts.com and other type libraries, and built a large business licensing fonts to brands and developers. In 2019 the private equity firm HGGC took Monotype private for about $825 million. Its fonts are still licensed to device makers, software companies and global brands.

cover.theme: a printer at work (type and printing)

tagline: A Comet Across the Booking Sky
dek: An online travel agency for flights, hotels and packages, first created by the major U.S. airlines.
lede: Orbitz sold flights, hotels and vacation packages online. The site began as a project of the major American airlines, which wanted their own answer to Expedia and Travelocity. By 2007 Orbitz Worldwide also included ebookers in Europe and HotelClub in Asia Pacific, and it was one of the largest online travel companies in the world. Its name was familiar to a generation of travelers.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Five big airlines formed the company in 1999 and launched the site in 2001. Their bet was that the airlines together could sell their own tickets online more cheaply than through outside agents. Orbitz won customers with a fast search engine and a clear display of fares. Travelport, owned by Blackstone, bought it in 2004 and later spun it out.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Orbitz Worldwide priced its IPO at $15 a share in July 2007 on the New York Stock Exchange. The recession and heavy debt soon pressed on the business, and the stock fell far below its offering price. In 2015 Expedia bought Orbitz for about $1.6 billion. Orbitz kept running as a separate brand within Expedia Group, alongside Travelocity and CheapTickets.

fate: Still public as DHI Group (NYSE: DHX)
tagline: A Roll of the Dice for Talent
dek: Online job boards for technology professionals and other specialist fields.
lede: Dice was where technology workers looked for jobs. Its job board listed openings for programmers, engineers and IT staff, and employers paid to post jobs and search its database of résumés. By 2007 Dice Holdings also owned boards for finance and energy professionals. It filed as the tech job market was strong and hiring was brisk. Its audience was narrow, but highly sought after.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Dice began in 1990 as an electronic bulletin board for computer contractors, years before the web. The bet was that specialists wanted a place built for their field, not a general job board. That focus let Dice charge employers more, because its audience was hard to reach any other way. Dice charged employers for job postings and résumé searches, while job seekers used the site free.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Dice Holdings priced its IPO at $13 a share in July 2007 on the New York Stock Exchange. Its business rose and fell with tech hiring, and LinkedIn became a strong rival for recruiters' budgets. The company renamed itself DHI Group and remains publicly traded. It later sold its finance and energy boards and returned its focus to technology careers.

dek: Measurement of internet audiences and online behavior, used by publishers and advertisers.
lede: Comscore measured who was doing what online. It recruited a large panel of internet users who agreed to have their browsing tracked, and sold the resulting data to websites, advertisers and investors. Its monthly rankings of the most visited sites became a standard reference. In 2007 online advertising was growing fast, and buyers wanted numbers they could trust. Its data also fed investor research on internet companies.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Gian Fulgoni and Magid Abraham, veterans of the market research firm Information Resources, founded Comscore in 1999. Their bet was that the internet needed a ratings system like television had, but based on far richer data about behavior. They built the panel first and then sold subscriptions to the reports. The panel let Comscore see not just traffic, but what people bought and searched for.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Comscore priced its IPO at $16.50 a share in June 2007 on the Nasdaq. In 2016 it merged with Rentrak to measure television too. Accounting problems led to its delisting in 2018 and a restatement, after which it returned to the Nasdaq. It remains publicly traded. Its business now centers on measuring audiences across television, streaming and digital media platforms.

dek: A content delivery network that carried video, downloads and web pages for large media and tech companies.
lede: Limelight Networks moved the internet's heaviest files. It ran a global network of servers that delivered video streams, software downloads and web pages quickly to users around the world. Its customers included major media and technology companies. In 2007 online video was exploding, and Limelight was the main challenger to Akamai, the leader in content delivery. Its customers ranged from video sites to software and game companies.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Limelight was founded in Arizona in 2001. Its bet was that a new network, built with large data centers and its own fiber links, could deliver rich media more cheaply than older designs. The company won big video customers early and grew quickly alongside them. It focused on video and large files, where speed and capacity mattered most. That focus brought fast growth, along with a few very large customers that made up much of its revenue.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Limelight priced its IPO at $15 a share in June 2007 on the Nasdaq. A patent lawsuit from Akamai, filed in 2006, dragged on for years. Pricing pressure kept profits thin. In 2022 Limelight bought Yahoo's Edgecast and renamed itself Edgio, which filed for bankruptcy in 2024. Through all of it, the company never matched the scale or profits of its larger rival.

cover.theme: a singer on the stage (the limelight)
cover.artwork: On the Stage, plate one from Yvette Guilbert

fate: Merged with Informa Tech, 2024; still public (NASDAQ: TTGT)
dek: Online publications for technology buyers, paid for by vendors seeking sales leads.
lede: TechTarget published websites for people who buy technology at work. Its many sites covered storage, security, networking and other topics in depth, and readers registered to download white papers and research. Technology vendors paid TechTarget to reach those readers and to receive leads on who was researching a purchase. In 2007 trade magazines were losing ground, and TechTarget's online model was taking their place.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Greg Strakosch and Don Hawk founded TechTarget in 1999. Their bet was that specialized content could attract IT professionals at the moment they were researching purchases, and that vendors would pay well to know who they were. The company built dozens of focused sites, each a target for a narrow group of buyers. Readers got free content, and vendors paid to reach them.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: TechTarget priced its IPO at $13 a share in May 2007 on the Nasdaq. It shifted further toward selling data on buying intent. In 2024 it combined with Informa Tech's digital businesses, and the new company, majority owned by Informa, kept the TechTarget name and listing. Its sites still serve IT buyers, and its data on who is researching what remains its main product.

dek: Equipment and software that let telephone carriers move voice calls onto internet-based networks.
lede: Veraz Networks sold gear that helped telephone companies move calls onto internet technology. Its switches, media gateways and voice compression products let carriers handle voice traffic over IP networks, cutting costs and adding services. Its customers were mostly phone carriers outside the United States. In 2007 carriers worldwide were in the middle of this long shift. Few consumers knew its name, but many international calls ran through equipment like it.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Veraz bet that telephone carriers would replace their old circuit switches with software-based equipment for internet calling. It combined that with voice compression technology, which carriers in developing markets valued for saving scarce bandwidth. The company had close ties to ECI Telecom, which owned a large stake. Its products were especially popular with carriers in emerging markets, where bandwidth was costly. Its main rivals were much larger equipment makers.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Veraz priced its IPO at $8 a share in April 2007 on the Nasdaq. Competition from larger equipment makers and the 2008 downturn hurt sales. In 2010 Veraz merged with Dialogic, a communications technology company, and the combined business took the Dialogic name. The merger was in effect a reverse acquisition, with Dialogic's owners holding most of the combined company.

cover.theme: a field telegraph wagon (the voice network)

dek: Enterprise Wi-Fi networks for offices, campuses and hospitals, managed from central controllers.
lede: Aruba Networks built the Wi-Fi inside large organizations. Its access points and central controllers let a university, hospital or corporate campus run thousands of wireless connections securely from one place. In 2007 laptops had made Wi-Fi a must, and the first iPhone was months away. Companies were deciding that wireless, not cables, would be how people connected at work. Hospitals, schools and offices were early customers.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Keerti Melkote and Pankaj Manglik founded Aruba in 2002. Their bet was that enterprise Wi-Fi needed central management and security, not standalone access points scattered around a building. Aruba competed directly with Cisco, which dominated networking, and won customers that needed large, mobile and secure wireless networks. Its design put the intelligence in a central controller, which made large networks easier to secure and manage.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Aruba priced its IPO at $11 a share in March 2007 on the Nasdaq. Smartphones and tablets soon flooded offices and campuses, and demand for its gear grew. In 2015 Hewlett-Packard bought Aruba for about $3 billion, and the Aruba name lived on as HP's networking brand. By then it had grown into a leading rival to Cisco in enterprise wireless networks. The Aruba brand remains at the center of HP's networking business.

dek: An online retailer of aftermarket car parts and accessories, sold through its own websites and marketplaces.
lede: U.S. Auto Parts sold replacement car parts online. Bumpers, headlights, mirrors and engine parts for thousands of makes and models were listed across its websites and on eBay, often at prices well below dealers and repair shops. It shipped from its own warehouses and sourced many products directly from manufacturers in Asia. It went public in early 2007, as do-it-yourself buyers were moving online.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: The company started in 1995 selling auto parts, and moved its business onto the internet. The bet was that car owners and small repair shops would buy parts online if the catalog was deep and the price was right. Matching the right part to the right vehicle was hard, and U.S. Auto Parts built its catalog data to solve it.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: U.S. Auto Parts priced its IPO at $10 a share in February 2007 on the Nasdaq. Search engine changes and competition hurt its traffic in the years that followed, and the stock spent long stretches at low levels. The company renamed itself CarParts.com in 2020 and remains publicly traded. The company later invested in new distribution centers to ship parts faster across the country.

cover.theme: a motor car in the street (car parts)

dek: An online university for working adults, focused on graduate degrees in business, education, psychology and health.
lede: Capella University taught working adults entirely online. Most of its students were mid-career and pursuing master's and doctoral degrees in fields like business, education, psychology and nursing. It was regionally accredited, which mattered to employers and students alike. When it went public in November 2006, online higher education was growing fast and drawing new investor interest. Its students came from every state and many countries.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Stephen Shank, a former chief executive of the toy company Tonka, founded Capella in 1991 as The Graduate School of America. The bet was that adults with jobs and families would pursue advanced degrees if they could study on their own schedule. Capella built its programs online from the start, rather than adapting a campus model. It later added competency-based programs that let students move at their own pace.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Capella priced its IPO at $20 a share in November 2006 on the Nasdaq. Enrollment grew for several years, then slowed under tighter federal rules for for-profit schools. In 2018 Capella merged with Strayer Education, and the combined company became Strategic Education. Capella University continues to operate as part of Strategic Education, alongside Strayer University. It remains one of the largest online universities in the country.

cover.theme: the fates among the stars (Capella, a bright star)
cover.artwork: The Fates Gathering in the Stars

tagline: At the Summit of the Network
dek: Session border controllers that secured and routed internet voice and video calls between carriers.
lede: Acme Packet made the gatekeepers of internet calling. Its session border controllers sat at the edges of carrier and enterprise networks, connecting voice and video calls between them, enforcing security and keeping the quality high. In 2006 telephone companies were moving their networks onto internet technology, and every border between networks needed a guard. Its main customers were telephone carriers and cable operators.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Andy Ory and Patrick MeLampy, who had worked together at earlier networking companies, founded Acme Packet in 2000. Their bet was that internet calling would need a dedicated device at each network border, and that carriers would pay for one built for the job. It became the leader in a category it helped define. Those early relationships with major carriers set the stage for rapid growth.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Acme Packet priced its IPO at $9.50 a share in October 2006 on the Nasdaq. It was profitable and grew quickly as carriers and large businesses adopted internet calling. In 2013 Oracle bought Acme Packet for about $2.1 billion. Oracle used the business as the base of its communications unit, selling the same products to carriers and large enterprises. Its products remain in use in many carrier networks.

dek: An online marketplace for buying health insurance, later focused on Medicare plans.
lede: eHealth let people shop for health insurance online. Its site, eHealthInsurance.com, showed plans from many insurers side by side, so individuals, families and small businesses could compare prices and coverage before they bought. The company was paid commissions by insurers. In 2006 most Americans got insurance through work, and those buying on their own had few easy ways to compare.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: eHealth started in 1997 with a bet that buying health insurance, a confusing and paper-heavy process, could work like other online shopping. It became a licensed broker in every state and built tools to quote and apply for plans online. Its customers were mostly people who bought insurance for themselves, such as the self-employed. Insurers paid it commissions for the policies it sold, much as they paid traditional agents.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: eHealth priced its IPO at $14 a share in October 2006 on the Nasdaq. The Affordable Care Act and its public exchanges later changed the individual market. eHealth turned toward Medicare plans for older Americans, which became most of its business. It remains publicly traded. Its Medicare business grew quickly as baby boomers aged into the program, though rising marketing costs and changing commissions made profits uneven.

cover.theme: lovers under an umbrella (coverage and protection)
cover.artwork: Lovers Beneath an Umbrella in the Snow

dek: Online photo printing and personalized photo books, cards and gifts.
lede: Shutterfly turned digital photos into things you could hold. As cameras went digital, people stopped printing film, and their pictures piled up on hard drives. Shutterfly let them upload photos, store them free and order prints, photo books, cards and calendars, made in its own plants. By 2006 photo books and holiday cards were its fastest-growing products. Its customers were mostly families saving their memories.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Shutterfly was founded in 1999 with backing from Netscape co-founder Jim Clark, and Eva Manolis was among its founders. The bet was that digital photography would create a large market for high-quality printed products. Shutterfly ran its own manufacturing to control quality, and it treated free storage as a way to keep customers coming back. Free unlimited photo storage was part of its offer from early on.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Shutterfly priced its IPO at $15 a share in September 2006 on the Nasdaq. It bought Tiny Prints and the school photo company Lifetouch, and its holiday season became a major retail event. In 2019 Apollo took Shutterfly private for about $2.7 billion. Its busiest weeks came each December, when holiday cards and photo gifts drove a large share of the year's sales.

dek: Data backup, recovery and management software for businesses, built on a single unified platform.
lede: CommVault protected the data of large organizations. Its software backed up, archived and recovered data across servers and storage systems, all from one platform and one index. Many rivals sold separate tools for each task. In 2006 corporate data was growing fast, and new rules required businesses to keep and find their records. Its customers included many large enterprises and public agencies.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: CommVault grew out of a data management group at Bell Labs and became an independent company in 1996. Its bet was that companies would want one integrated system for every kind of data protection, instead of a patchwork. It sold mainly through partners such as Dell and storage resellers. Its single code base and shared index set it apart from rivals that stitched together products from acquisitions.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: CommVault priced its IPO at $14.50 a share in September 2006 on the Nasdaq. It grew into one of the leading backup software companies. Later it moved its products to the cloud and added protection against ransomware. It remains publicly traded. Its customers include large enterprises and government agencies around the world. Many of them first bought its software for basic backup and later used it for archiving and compliance.

cover.artwork: The Giant Wheel, plate 9 from Imaginary Prisons

dek: Network appliances that sped up applications running over wide area networks between offices.
lede: Riverbed made far-away offices feel close. Its Steelhead appliances sat at each end of a company's wide area network and cut the data crossing it, so files and applications opened quickly in branch offices. In 2006 companies were pulling servers back into central data centers to save money, and slow links to remote offices had become a daily complaint. Its customers ranged from law firms to global manufacturers.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Jerry Kennelly and Steve McCanne, a computer scientist known for internet video research, founded Riverbed in 2002. Their bet was that smarter software, not more bandwidth, could fix slow networks. Riverbed combined data deduplication and protocol tricks in a box that was easy to install, and sales grew quickly. Customers often saw results in days, which made the boxes an easy sale.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Riverbed priced its IPO at $9.75 a share in September 2006 on the Nasdaq and soon traded well above it. It led the WAN optimization market for years. As applications moved to the cloud, growth slowed, and in 2015 Thoma Bravo took Riverbed private for about $3.6 billion. It went through a debt restructuring in 2021, and still sells network performance tools.

tagline: The Eye That Sees Every Click
dek: Web analytics software that showed companies how visitors used their websites.
lede: Omniture showed companies what happened on their websites. Its SiteCatalyst service tracked every page view and click, so marketers could see where visitors came from, what they did and what they bought. It sold to large retailers and media companies by subscription. In 2006 online sales were booming, and measuring them had become a job for serious software. Its customers included many of the largest retailers online.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Josh James and John Pestana, two young Utah entrepreneurs, founded the company in 1996. Their bet was that businesses would want detailed, real-time data on their online customers, and would pay for it as a hosted service. Omniture won large clients and later added tools for testing and targeting. Its customers paid by volume, so its revenue grew as their websites grew.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Omniture priced its IPO at $6.50 a share in June 2006 on the Nasdaq. It grew quickly and bought several rivals, including WebSideStory and Visual Sciences. In 2009 Adobe bought Omniture for about $1.8 billion, and its software became the core of Adobe's marketing business. Omniture's analytics live on today as Adobe Analytics, part of its Experience Cloud. The deal set Adobe on the road to its large marketing software business.

cover.artwork: The Eye, Like a Strange Balloon Moves Towards Infinity, plate one from To Edgar Poe

dek: An online marketplace for listing and finding commercial real estate for sale or lease.
lede: LoopNet was the listings site for commercial property. Brokers posted offices, shops, warehouses and apartment buildings for sale or lease, and buyers and tenants searched them free or with premium memberships. It became the largest marketplace of its kind in the United States. When it went public in 2006, commercial real estate was booming. It also offered data on property sales and comparables.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Dennis DeAndre started LoopNet in San Francisco in 1995. The bet was that commercial real estate, a business of private networks and printed flyers, would move its listings online. LoopNet let brokers list for free and charged the heaviest users for premium features, which grew a large base of listings quickly. Its free listings drew the scale that rivals could not match.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: LoopNet priced its IPO at $12 a share in June 2006 on the Nasdaq. It stayed profitable through the property downturn of 2008 and 2009. In 2012 CoStar, the commercial property data company, bought LoopNet for about $860 million after regulators approved the deal. LoopNet continues to run as a CoStar brand, and its listings remain a standard stop for commercial property searches.

tagline: Setting Sail on a New Line
dek: Home phone service over broadband internet, sold at a flat monthly price.
lede: Vonage turned the home phone into an internet service. Customers plugged a small adapter into their broadband connection and kept a regular phone number, with unlimited calling across the country for a flat monthly fee. Its ads were everywhere, and by 2006 it had more than a million and a half subscribers. It was the best-known challenger to the old phone companies, and the cable companies were coming for the same customers.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Jeffrey Citron, a former electronic trading entrepreneur, started Vonage in 2001. The bet was that broadband homes would drop expensive landline plans for internet calling if it felt just like a normal phone. Vonage spent heavily on marketing to win customers fast, and it lost a lot of money doing so. Its price, a flat monthly fee for unlimited calls, undercut traditional phone plans by a wide margin.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Vonage priced its IPO at $17 a share in May 2006 on the New York Stock Exchange. The stock fell on its first day and kept falling, and customers who had been offered shares in the deal were angry. Patent suits from Verizon added to its trouble. Vonage later rebuilt itself around business communications, and Ericsson bought it in 2022 for about $6.2 billion.

dek: Online auction marketplaces for surplus and returned goods from governments and large companies.
lede: Liquidity Services sold what others no longer needed. It ran online auctions for surplus and returned goods, from excess inventory at big retailers to used vehicles and equipment from government agencies. Its biggest early contract was selling U.S. military surplus. When it filed in 2006, it was turning a dusty corner of commerce into a steady online business. Buyers ranged from small resellers to large exporters.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: William Angrick founded the company in 1999. The bet was that surplus goods, usually sold in slow local auctions or scrapped, would fetch better prices online in front of many more buyers. Liquidity Services won large contracts with the Defense Department and built sites such as Liquidation.com and GovDeals. Its sellers paid a share of each sale, so the company earned more as prices rose.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Liquidity Services priced its IPO at $10 a share in February 2006 on the Nasdaq. It grew for years on its military surplus contracts, then lost some of them, and the stock swung widely. The company refocused on retail returns and government surplus. It remains publicly traded. Its marketplaces still handle large volumes of surplus goods from public agencies and retailers.

cover.theme: the clothes exchange after the sale (surplus)
cover.artwork: After the Sale, Clothes Exchange, Houndsditch

dek: Overnight radiology reading for U.S. hospitals, done by American doctors working in daytime abroad.
lede: NightHawk Radiology read X-rays and CT scans while American radiologists slept. Hospitals sent their overnight emergency images over the internet to U.S.-trained, U.S.-licensed radiologists working in Sydney and Zurich, where it was daytime. Reports came back in minutes. In 2006 emergency rooms were scanning more patients than ever, and small radiology groups struggled to cover every night. Its doctors worked days abroad and read scans for hospitals across the country.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Paul Berger, a radiologist in Idaho, co-founded NightHawk in 2001. The bet was that time zones could solve the overnight staffing problem, and that radiology groups would gladly pay to give their doctors a full night's sleep. The company handled licensing and credentials across many states, which was the hard part. Its radiologists held licenses in many states at once.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: NightHawk priced its IPO at $16 a share in February 2006 on the Nasdaq. Competition and pricing pressure grew, and many radiology groups began to cover nights themselves. In 2010 Virtual Radiologic bought NightHawk for about $170 million. The combined company, under the vRad name, became the largest teleradiology provider in the United States. Its overnight model is now standard practice in American hospitals.

tagline: Reading the Flow of the City
dek: Real-time traffic information gathered from road sensors and delivered to drivers, broadcasters and navigation systems.
lede: Traffic.com told drivers where the jams were. It installed its own sensors along major roads in dozens of American cities, combined that data with other sources and sent live traffic reports to radio and TV stations, websites, phones and in-car navigation. In early 2006 GPS devices were spreading fast, and live traffic was the feature everyone wanted next. Its reports reached millions of listeners each day.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Traffic.com began in 1998 with a bet that accurate, real-time traffic data would be valuable to many outlets at once. Building its own sensor network gave it data rivals did not have. It earned money from licensing that data and from selling advertising in the traffic reports it produced for broadcasters. Selling the same data many times over was the core of its plan.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Traffic.com priced its IPO at $12 a share in January 2006 on the Nasdaq. The company struggled to turn its costly sensor network into a profit. Within a year Navteq, the digital map maker, agreed to buy it, and the deal closed in 2007 at about $179 million. Navteq, later bought by Nokia, folded its traffic data into the maps used by car navigation systems.

dek: An online network linking car dealers with auto lenders, plus software to run the dealership.
lede: DealerTrack connected car dealers to the banks that financed their customers. Before it, a dealer faxed a buyer's credit application to lenders one at a time. DealerTrack's network let the dealer send it to many lenders at once and get answers back in minutes. By 2005 a large share of American franchised dealers used it, and the company was selling more software to run the rest of the dealership.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: DealerTrack was formed in 2001 with backing from several large auto lenders. The bet was that a neutral online network for credit applications would speed up car sales for everyone. Lenders paid a fee for each application, and dealers signed on because the system was simple and saved time on the showroom floor. Its scale soon became an advantage, since every new lender made the network more useful to dealers.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: DealerTrack priced its IPO at $17 a share in December 2005 on the Nasdaq. It grew through many acquisitions, adding dealer management systems, compliance tools and Dealer.com. In 2015 Cox Automotive bought DealerTrack for about $4 billion. Cox combined it with brands such as Autotrader and Kelley Blue Book, building one of the largest companies in automotive software. Many dealers still use its tools today.

dek: Online public relations software for managing media lists, press releases and news monitoring.
lede: Vocus gave public relations teams their software. Its online service kept databases of journalists and outlets, sent press releases, tracked news coverage and measured results, all in a web browser. It sold to corporations, agencies and government offices by subscription. In 2005, PR work still ran largely on phone calls and spreadsheets, and the move to online tools was just starting.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Rick Rudman and Bob Lentz founded the company in 1992. They bet that public relations, a craft run on personal contacts, would adopt software for its daily work. Vocus moved to a hosted subscription model early, and later bought PRWeb, the online press release service. Its customers ranged from small agencies to large corporations and government offices. Subscriptions made its revenue steady and predictable.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Vocus priced its IPO at $9 a share in December 2005 on the Nasdaq. It grew steadily and added marketing tools for small businesses, with mixed results. In 2014 the private equity firm GTCR took Vocus private for about $446 million and combined it with Cision. The combined company kept the Cision name and became one of the largest providers of public relations software in the world.

tagline: The Doctor Will See You Online
dek: The leading consumer health information website, funded by advertising from drug makers and health companies.
lede: WebMD was where Americans went to look up their symptoms. Its site explained conditions, drugs and treatments in plain language, and its sister site Medscape served doctors. Pharmaceutical and health companies paid to advertise to these readers. In 2005 the company was a unit of Emdeon, the former Healtheon/WebMD, and this offering sold a minority stake in its online health business.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: WebMD came out of the dot-com era, when Jeff Arnold founded it in 1998 and it merged with Jim Clark's Healtheon. The early dream was to wire the whole health care system. What lasted was simpler: a trusted source of health information for consumers, paid for by advertising and sponsorships. Its consumer site and Medscape together gave it reach to both patients and doctors.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: WebMD Health priced its IPO at $17.50 a share in September 2005 on the Nasdaq. It later became fully independent of its parent and stayed the top health site for years. In 2017 Internet Brands, owned by KKR, bought WebMD for about $2.8 billion. The site remains one of the most visited health information sources in the United States. Its brand is still widely known.

dek: Transaction processing, data and reservation technology for travel agencies and corporate travel programs.
lede: TRX worked behind the scenes of business travel. It processed bookings and transactions for travel agencies and corporate travel managers, provided reservation and customer support services, and offered data tools that showed companies how their employees traveled. In 2005 online booking was spreading, and travel agencies were outsourcing more of their back-office work. Its customers included large travel agencies and corporations.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: TRX bet that travel agencies and corporations would hand off the routine, high-volume work of processing travel to a specialist. It combined hosted technology with call centers and processing staff. Over time it put more weight on travel data, helping companies track spending and negotiate with airlines and hotels. Its corporate travel data business showed companies where their money went and where they could save.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: TRX priced its IPO at $9 a share in September 2005 on the Nasdaq. It spent several years as a small public company while it shifted toward travel data. In 2013 Concur, the travel and expense software maker, acquired TRX. Concur, which SAP bought the following year, folded TRX's travel data tools into its own corporate travel products. Its data tools lived on inside Concur.

dek: A regional phone and internet carrier serving small and midsize businesses in the western United States.
lede: Eschelon Telecom sold phone lines, internet access and phone systems to small and midsize businesses. It operated in cities across the West and Midwest, from Minneapolis to Seattle and Phoenix, competing with the large regional Bell company. It filed to go public in 2005, after the telecom crash had wiped out many of its peers. Its customers were mostly small and midsize businesses in growing cities.

sections.heading: The Original Bet
sections.body: Eschelon began in 1996, soon after the Telecommunications Act opened local phone markets to competition. Its bet was that small businesses wanted one local provider with good service for all their communications. It leased parts of the incumbent's network and bundled phone equipment with its lines. Like many competitive carriers of its era, it depended on access rules that regulators could change.

sections.heading: After the Offering
sections.body: Eschelon priced its IPO at $14 a share in August 2005 on the Nasdaq. It grew through acquisitions of smaller carriers. In 2007 Integra Telecom bought Eschelon for about $710 million, including debt. The merger made Integra one of the largest competitive carriers in the western United States. The Eschelon name faded as its customers and networks were folded into Integra.
